visual.question: Which failure would you investigate first?

chapters.title: Hook and introduction
chapters.text: Imagine your team has spent three months developing a mobile application. The design looks perfect, the developers are confident, and the client is excited. But one day before launch, your testing team discovers that users cannot complete their payments. The launch gets delayed, development costs increase, and customer confidence suffers. Now imagine discovering the same issue during the first week of development. That is exactly where Agile Testing makes a difference. Welcome to this lesson. We will explain what Agile Testing is, how it differs from traditional testing, and how software teams apply it in practice.
chapters.direction: Show a launch countdown, failed payment screen and a team identifying the issue early.

chapters.title: What is Agile Testing?
chapters.text: Agile Testing is an approach in which testing happens continuously throughout software development. Rather than waiting for developers to finish an entire application, testers collaborate with them from the beginning. Consider an e-commerce website. In the first sprint, developers implement login while testers prepare scenarios for valid credentials, incorrect passwords, empty fields and security. In the next sprint, the team builds a shopping cart, and testers verify both the new feature and existing login behavior. This process continues throughout delivery. The key idea is to identify problems early, resolve them quickly, and continuously improve the product. Let us make that difference concrete. Suppose a customer has one thousand rupees in a wallet and purchases an item costing three hundred rupees. The expected remaining balance is seven hundred. That arithmetic is simple, but the workflow raises more questions. What if the request is submitted twice? What if the payment service accepts it but the browser loses the response? A good testing conversation identifies those risks before the team commits to one implementation. Early testing includes asking useful questions, not just running a finished application.
chapters.direction: Animated cycle: Plan → Develop → Test → Feedback → Plan.

chapters.title: Agile versus traditional testing
chapters.text: In a typical Waterfall project, work moves through sequential phases: requirements, design, implementation and testing. Major defects may remain undiscovered until late in delivery. Agile works differently. Development and testing take place together in short iterations, commonly called sprints. Testers collaborate with developers, Product Owners and stakeholders throughout the process. Frequent feedback allows teams to adjust priorities. If a customer requests a discount feature, the team can clarify it, prioritize it and validate it in an upcoming sprint. The objective is not merely to work faster but to validate that the team is building the right product at the right quality level.
chapters.direction: Side-by-side Waterfall sequence and iterative Agile feedback loops.

chapters.title: Five core principles
chapters.text: First, continuous testing means that quality is evaluated throughout development. Second, shared responsibility means developers, testers and other team members contribute to quality. Third, early feedback enables problems to be investigated before additional work depends on them. Fourth, customer collaboration ensures regular feedback on real business needs. Fifth, working software matters: a feature is not complete merely because coding has finished. It should satisfy agreed acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done. Together, these principles encourage teams to build quality into the product instead of treating testing as a final inspection. Here is a small acceptance example you can use in a team discussion. Given an account with a registered email address, when the customer requests a password reset, then a single-use link is sent and the account remains protected. Now add two variations: a link that has expired, and a link that has already been used. Agree on the expected outcomes before coding. Notice how one short example reveals several design decisions. Also consider whether the response could reveal which email addresses have accounts; avoid exposing that information unnecessarily.
chapters.direction: Five animated principle cards with one practical example each.

chapters.title: Agile Testing in Scrum
chapters.text: Consider a two-week Scrum sprint. During Sprint Planning, the team selects Product Backlog Items supporting a Sprint Goal. A user story might say: As a customer, I want to reset my password so that I can regain access to my account. Before development, the team clarifies acceptance criteria. What happens if the address is unregistered? When does the reset link expire? What happens if the link is reused? During the sprint, developers implement the functionality while testers prepare and execute checks. The team resolves defects collaboratively. At the Sprint Review, stakeholders inspect the increment and provide feedback. At the Retrospective, the team identifies improvements to its process.
chapters.direction: Sprint board: Backlog → In Progress → Testing → Done; add review and retrospective.

chapters.title: Four Agile Testing quadrants
chapters.text: The four Agile Testing quadrants help teams choose complementary kinds of testing. Quadrant one focuses on technology-facing tests supporting development, such as unit and component tests. Quadrant two includes business-facing examples and acceptance tests that guide development. Quadrant three evaluates the product from a user and business perspective, including exploratory and usability testing. Quadrant four examines technical qualities such as performance, security and reliability. In a banking application, a unit test can check interest calculations, an acceptance test can check money transfers, exploratory testing can reveal confusing interactions, and load testing can examine heavy usage. The quadrants are not sequential phases. Try this classification exercise. A calculation test runs without opening a browser. A customer evaluates whether checkout instructions make sense. A team measures response time under concurrent traffic. These activities investigate different risks, so one cannot replace the others. The calculation test gives precise, fast feedback about a rule. Customer observation explores whether the product supports a real task. Load testing examines behavior under stress. A balanced strategy chooses enough of each for the product's circumstances, rather than treating the number of automated checks as a complete measure of quality.
chapters.direction: Display a labelled two-by-two quadrant matrix with concrete examples.

chapters.title: Real-world example
chapters.text: Imagine a food delivery application. Sprint one delivers registration and login. The tester checks valid and invalid credentials, recovery and security scenarios. Sprint two introduces restaurant listings and search; testers examine accuracy, filters and empty results. Sprint three adds the shopping cart and payment integration. The team tests payment success, payment failure, duplicate transactions and order confirmation. Importantly, it also verifies that previously completed functionality still works. This is regression testing. Continuous testing across sprints reduces the chance that major problems are discovered only before release. Before you move on, write a miniature test plan for a login feature. Include one successful login, one invalid-password attempt, one session-expiry check, and one access-control check after logout. For every check, state both the input and the observable outcome. Avoid saying only that login should work; specify what a legitimate user can see and what an unauthenticated person must not see. This exercise turns a general quality goal into a practical conversation. Keep your plan, because later lessons will add techniques, artifacts and automation to the same reasoning.
chapters.direction: Three sprint timeline with login, search, and cart/payment; show regression checks across sprints.

chapters.title: Tools and automation
chapters.text: Tools can support fast feedback. Jira can track user stories, bugs and sprint progress. Postman can validate A P I services. Selenium and Playwright can automate browser testing. Appium supports mobile automation, and Jenkins or GitHub Actions can run tests in continuous integration pipelines. Automation is useful for repetitive checks, but it does not replace human investigation. Exploratory testing still depends on judgment and curiosity. Choose tools based on risks, technology and testing needs. The goal is not to automate everything; it is to obtain useful, reliable feedback efficiently.
chapters.direction: Tool categories and a simple CI pipeline; avoid implying that any tool guarantees quality.

chapters.title: Recap and outro
chapters.text: Agile Testing is continuous and collaborative. Testing begins early and continues throughout development. Scrum creates regular opportunities for planning, inspection and improvement. The testing quadrants help balance business and technical quality, while automation makes repetitive checks more efficient. The most important takeaway is that quality is not added at the end; it is built into every stage of delivery. In the next episode, we will compare Agile methodologies in greater detail. Knowledge check: why can identifying a defect during the first sprint be less costly than discovering it just before launch? Subscribe to Tech at sixty for the next episode in this Agile Testing Masterclass. Practice the example with synthetic data, and share the most important risk you identified in the comments.
